content: Bacterial meningitis is a serious infection of the central nervous system that requires prompt and targeted antimicrobial therapy. The choice of empiric therapy depends on the patient’s age, underlying conditions, and specific risk factors. Below is a detailed breakdown of the recommended treatments based on these factors: Age-Specific Recommendations 1. Neonates (<1 month old): Common pathogens: Streptococcus agalactiae, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and Klebsiella species. Preferred regimen: Intravenous (IV) ampicillin at 12 g/day every 4 hours, combined with either cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours), amikacin (15 mg/kg/day every 8 hours), gentamicin (5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours), or tobramycin (5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours). 2. Infants (1–23 months): Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Escherichia coli. Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). 3. Children and Adults (2–50 years): Common pathogens: Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). 4. Older Adults (>50 years): Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes, and aerobic Gram-negative bacilli. Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours) and either ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). Trauma-Related Meningitis 1. Basilar Skull Fracture: Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and group A β-hemolytic streptococci. Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). 2. Penetrating Trauma: Common pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis), and aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either cefepime (6 g/day every 8 hours), ceftazidime (6 g/day every 8 hours), or meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours). 3. Postneurosurgery: Common pathogens: Aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa), Staphylococcus aureus, and coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis). Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either cefepime (6 g/day every 8 hours), ceftazidime (6 g/day every 8 hours), or meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours). 4. Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Shunt Infections: Common pathogens: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis), Staphylococcus aureus, aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa), and Propionibacterium acnes. Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either cefepime (6 g/day every 8 hours), ceftazidime (6 g/day every 8 hours), or meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours). CSF Gram Stain-Directed Therapy 1. Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci (suggestive of Streptococcus pneumoniae): Preferred regimen: IV vancomycin at 30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours, combined with either ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). Alternative regimen: Meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours), gatifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours), or moxifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours). 2. Gram-negative diplococci (suggestive of Neisseria meningitidis): Preferred regimen: Ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). Alternative regimen: Penicillin G (24 MU/day every 4 hours), ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours), chloramphenicol (4–6 g/day every 6 hours), gatifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours), moxifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours), or aztreonam (6–8 g/day every 6–8 hours). 3. Gram-positive, short bacilli (suggestive of Listeria monocytogenes): Preferred regimen: Ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours) or penicillin G (24 MU/day every 4 hours), with or without amikacin (15 mg/kg/day every 8 hours), gentamicin (5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours), or tobramycin (5 mg/kg/day every 8 hours). Alternative regimen: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (10–20 mg/kg/day every 6–12 hours) or meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours). 4. Gram-negative bacilli (suggestive of Escherichia coli): Preferred regimen: Ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). Alternative regimen: Cefepime (6 g/day every 8 hours), meropenem (6 g/day every 8 hours), aztreonam (6–8 g/day every 6–8 hours), gatifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours), moxifloxacin (400 mg/day every 24 hours), or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (10–20 mg/kg/day every 6–12 hours). Pathogen-Directed Therapy 1. Streptococcus pneumoniae: Penicillin MIC <0.1 μg/mL: Penicillin G (24 MU/day every 4 hours) or ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours). Penicillin MIC 0.1–1.0 μg/mL: Ceftriaxone (4 g/day every 12–24 hours) or cefotaxime (8–12 g/day every 4–6 hours). Penicillin MIC ≥2.0 μg/mL or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime MIC ≥1.0 μg/mL: Vancomycin (30–45 mg/kg/day every 8–12 hours) combined with ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. 2. Neisseria meningitidis: Penicillin MIC <0.1 μg/mL: Penicillin G (24 MU/day every 4 hours) or ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours). Penicillin MIC 0.1–1.0 μg/mL: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. 3. Listeria monocytogenes: Preferred regimen: Ampicillin (12 g/day every 4 hours) or penicillin G (24 MU/day every 4 hours). Alternative regimen: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or meropenem. 4. Staphylococcus aureus: Methicillin-susceptible: Nafcillin (9–12 g/day every 4 hours) or oxacillin (9–12 g/day every 4 hours). Methicillin-resistant: Vancomycin.
